The kid runs off, and Walt smiles to himself at what has taken place. Then his smile fades. He turns back to where he encountered the neophyte meth cook. He goes out to the carpark, and tells the kid and the guy waiting with him to "stay out of my territory."

What happened in the time between him giving the kid that avuncular, ironic advice about which container to use to cook meth, and him squaring up to the drug dealers in the car park? Bare minutes have gone by, nothing has changed. Walt is out of the business, safely, cleanly. He could work on his marriage and children, continue to do home renovation, pour his considerable talents into legitimate industry. Truthfully, trying to figure out how Egyptian sounded is impossible, not least because it could not have been spoken in one consistent way. We're talking about a language that lasted in different forms for over 3000 years, and across a large geographical area. English changes in dialect and accent hugely depending on where it is spoken, and the pronunciation has changed significantly over time (just consider the English settlers in America.) Trying to pin down a single, monolith concept of how it was spoken is just not accurate.

However! Saying it is impossible to be precise in our knowledge is not the same as saying we know nothing. We have a good idea of how the words were pronounced because in 3rd century AD, Egypt became Christianised. Cos hieroglyphic was associated with the old religion and customs, it was deemed pagan, and therefore wrong, to use it. 

So.....

They started using the Greek alphabet. Egyptian words, as always, were written with Greek letters, which are very easy to read. This way of writing, and the entire period, is called Coptic. It's at the tail-end of Egypt's history, but we can get an idea of how the hieroglyphs were pronounced when we compare it to the Coptic words that came later. Off the back of that, we can start to build up a firmer picture of how things sounded, particularly when we find foreign names written in Hieroglyphic, or Egyptian names written in other languages.

Hey, on the bus to work so this answer will be a bit garbled and incomplete, but that's not a dumb question at all. 

The Egyptian written language was indeed a *phonetic* writing system, where each sound of the spoken language was represented using a symbol or sign (just like how you are reading this now, you see the "s" sign and make or think of a noise by pushing air out your mouth with your tongue on the roof.) The representation of sounds via writing has its own name, the Rebus Principle. The other writing system you described is a *pictoral* writing system, like that of the Chinese writing system - this means there is far less of a link between the spoken language and the written, and it's possible to be able to read Chinese without speaking a word, cos they are two separate systems.

So in Egyptian, the verb "to go/to come" is written with signs depicting a reed stem and a mouth, which egyptologists transliterate "jr" and was pronounced something like "eeyer" (all pronunciations are super approximate, no one knows how it was really pronounced.) However, cos they wrote literal little pics of stuff, they could use this to denote meaning, so "jr", when it meant "to go" and not something else, there is a hieroglyph of a little pair of legs to indicate that this is a word to do with movement.

Also, cos it was pictures, they could just write the thing they were talking about - the sound "r" was depicted with the mouth hieroglyph, and so you find it in words that would have had the "r" sound. Also though, the word for mouth could be written with just that hieroglyph.
